summary: A status report on the network numbers and autonomous system numbers used in the Internet community.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1166 describes how Internet addresses are divided into network and local parts, and records assigned network and autonomous-system numbers. Its tables capture assignments at the time of publication, not a live directory.

subtitle: A July 1990 record of assigned Internet network numbers and gateway autonomous-system numbers.

tldr.problem: Internet Protocol addresses need network numbers, and the Exterior Gateway Protocol uses numbers to identify autonomous systems. This memo records the assignments and the people responsible for them.
tldr.mechanism: It describes the parts of a 32-bit Internet address, then lists network numbers and autonomous-system numbers with names and contact references.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a dated assignment list, intended to be updated periodically. RFC 1166 was later updated by RFC 5737.

sections.title: What the Memo Records
sections.content:
RFC 1166 is a status report on assigned Internet network numbers and gateway autonomous systems. It says the memo will be updated periodically and directs readers seeking current information to Hostmaster at the DDN Network Information Center.

The entries identify the network or system and include a bracketed reference. The reference points to a document and to the responsible person's NIC Handle, a unique identifier used by the NIC WHOIS/NICNAME service. The memo says that service can provide current mailbox or phone details for an individual.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo records network numbers and gateway-system numbers assigned at the time. Each entry also points to a document and to a contact identifier.

sections.title: How Address Classes Divide 32 Bits
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) uses a 32-bit address divided into a network number and a local address part. RFC 1166 describes four address classes. Class A uses 7 network bits and 24 local bits; class B uses 14 network bits and 16 local bits; class C uses 21 network bits and 8 local bits.

The leading bits identify the class: class A begins with 0, class B with 1-0, and class C with 1-1-0. The memo says these formats allow 128 class A networks, 16,384 class B networks and 2,097,152 class C networks. Class D is used for multicast and begins with 1-1-1-0. Addresses beginning with 1-1-1-1, called class E, are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: An IP address has a network part and a local part. The first bits show which class format it uses, and each format gives those parts different sizes.

sections.title: Address Notation and Registry Marks
sections.content:
The memo writes addresses in dotted decimal: four 8-bit fields shown as decimal numbers separated by periods. It gives 128.9.0.32 as an example and uses nnn for network-number fields and rrr for local-address fields in its tables.

Each network entry may have a category letter: R for Research, D for Defense, G for Government (non-defense), or C for Commercial. An asterisk before a number marks an independent network. The memo says its administrators must apply separately for permission to interconnect with the Internet, and those networks should not appear in the working tables of Internet hosts or gateways. During a number change, the old entry may remain for a transition period, marked with T and a name ending in -TEMP.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables write addresses as four decimal fields separated by dots. Letters identify user categories; a star marks an independent network, and T marks a temporary old-number entry.

sections.title: Addresses with Special Meanings
sections.content:
In some contexts, an address has a function rather than identifying one host. An address of zero means “this,” such as this network; the memo gives 0.0.0.37 as an example of host 37 on this network. An address of all ones means “all”; 128.9.255.255 is its example for all hosts on network 128.9.

Network number 127 is assigned the loopback function. Data sent by a higher-level protocol to a network 127 address should loop back inside the host, and the memo says it should never appear on any network. The registry also marks 224.000.000.000-239.255.255.255 as multicast and 240.000.000.000-255.255.255.255 as reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Some addresses name a function instead of one host. Zero can mean “this,” all ones can mean “all,” and network 127 is reserved for traffic that loops back inside its host.

sections.title: The Network Number Listings
sections.content:
Most of RFC 1166 consists of class A, B and C network-number tables. Entries give an address or address range, a network name and a reference; the category letters and independent-network mark explain how an entry is classified. The tables include assigned entries as well as entries marked Reserved or Unassigned.

For example, the class A table labels network 10 ARPANET, 26 MILNET and 44 AMPRNET, while network 127 is Loopback. The class B and C tables continue the same registry format across their address ranges.
sections.plainLanguage: The largest part of the memo is a set of network tables. Each row associates an address or range with a name and a reference, and some rows are marked unassigned or reserved.

sections.title: Counts in the July 1990 Tables
sections.content:
The Network Totals section counts assignments in three ways. For networks assigned to the ARPA-Internet and DDN-Internet, it reports 29 class A, 1,209 class B and 2,972 class C networks, for a total of 4,210.

For numbers allocated for Internet and independent uses together, it reports 34 class A, 2,533 class B and 16,214 class C, for a total of 18,781. A separate maximum-allowed table lists 126 class A, 16,382 class B and 2,097,150 class C networks. These are the memo's counts, not present-day totals.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo counts networks in different assignment groups and lists the maximum allowed in each class. These figures describe the tables in this document, not today's assignments.

sections.title: Autonomous-System Numbers
sections.content:
The Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) describes groups of gateways that may form autonomous systems. EGP provides a 16-bit field to identify these systems, and RFC 1166 records the registered values.

The table pairs each number, or number range, with a system name and a contact reference. For example, the first entries assign 1 to The BBN Core Gateways, 2 to DCN-AS, 3 to The MIT Gateways and 4 to ISI-AS.
sections.plainLanguage: EGP uses a number to identify an autonomous system, a group of gateways. This memo lists those numbers beside system names and contact references.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section says that security issues are not discussed in this memo. RFC 1166 is a report on assigned network and autonomous-system numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not discuss security issues. It reports assigned network and autonomous-system numbers.

sections.title: Publication and Later Update
sections.content:
RFC 1166 was published in July 1990 as an Informational memo. Its introduction says that the list would be updated periodically, and the unit metadata records RFC 5737 as an RFC that later updated it.

The assignment tables therefore belong to the date and scope of this memo. They should not be read as a live list of current network or autonomous-system assignments.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1166 is an Informational memo from July 1990, and RFC 5737 later updated it. Its tables record the assignments in this older snapshot.
